dx_agent: Purulent (MRSA) pericarditis complicating MRSA bloodstream infection, with cardiac tamponade and cardiogenic shock, and associated myocardial involvement (new left-ventricular wall-motion abnormalities)
reasoning: The patient developed new chest pain during inpatient treatment for a bloodstream infection, and examination documented rapid hemodynamic deterioration with cardiogenic shock. Blood cultures confirmed MRSA bacteremia — an organism with a well-recognized propensity to seed the pericardial space and myocardium. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a pericardial effusion that progressed to cardiac tamponade, together with new left-ventricular wall-motion abnormalities, indicating concomitant myocardial involvement (myopericarditis and/or septic coronary embolism). Emergency pericardiocentesis yielded yellowish, turbid fluid, i.e. frank pus, which establishes the effusion as purulent rather than a sterile, reactive, uremic, malignant, or viral exudate. The combination of purulent pericardial fluid, documented MRSA bacteremia, tamponade physiology, new regional wall-motion abnormality, and shock unifies the entire presentation into a single infectious process. Competing diagnoses are excluded: isolated septic myocarditis or septic-embolus myocardial infarction would not produce a purulent tamponading effusion; pulmonary embolism cannot explain turbid pericardial fluid with MRSA bacteremia; and a non-infectious pericarditis is inconsistent with pus on pericardiocentesis in a bacteremic patient. Management requires urgent and often repeated surgical pericardial drainage (pericardial window/subxiphoid pericardiotomy for loculated pus), targeted intravenous anti-MRSA therapy with susceptibility-guided dosing, hemodynamic support, removal of any intravascular catheter source, and surveillance echocardiography to exclude concomitant infective endocarditis.

dx_agent: Persistent atrial standstill with complete AV block and junctional escape bradycardia (42/min), causing bradycardia-induced heart failure — isolated post-capillary pulmonary hypertension with severe tricuspid regurgitation, right ventricular dysfunction and right-sided heart failure (peripheral edema, pleural effusions, congestive hepatopathy)
reasoning:
The patient presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, leg edema and abdominal pain. Examination documented peripheral edema and marked bradycardia (42/min).

RHYTHM DIAGNOSIS — ATRIAL STANDSTILL: The surface ECG showed no P waves with a narrow-QRS escape rhythm at 42/min. Right-heart catheterization demonstrated no A wave in the wedge tracing, proving absent atrial mechanical systole. The electrophysiology study was definitive: an electrically silent right atrium with no response to coronary-sinus pacing (i.e., neither right nor left atrium could be depolarized) plus complete AV block. Cardiac MRI showed left atrial late gadolinium enhancement with borderline T1/T2 edema and no ventricular scar, identifying extensive atrial fibrosis as the anatomic substrate. The triad of absent P waves, absent A waves, and inexcitable atrial myocardium establishes persistent atrial standstill with associated complete AV block and a junctional escape rhythm.

HEMODYNAMIC CONSEQUENCES: With a heart rate of 42/min and a preserved cardiac output of 5.8 L/min, the stroke volume is approximately 138 mL. This large volume is ejected into a scarred, non-compliant left atrium that has lost both reservoir and booster-pump function, generating giant wedge V waves to 65 mmHg and a mean wedge pressure of 28 mmHg. Critically, the PVR was only 1.2 Wood units with a transpulmonary gradient of 7 mmHg (mPAP 35 − PCWP 28), proving isolated post-capillary pulmonary hypertension — the pulmonary vasculature is intrinsically normal and the elevated pressures are transmitted passively from the left atrium. CTPA excluded chronic thromboembolic disease (no pulmonary embolus), ruling out CTEPH.

RIGHT HEART FAILURE: The chronic backward transmission of pressure produced RV dilatation with impaired RV function and severe tricuspid regurgitation (echo PA systolic pressure 58 mmHg), with systemic venous congestion evidenced by contrast reflux into the hepatic veins and bilateral pleural effusions on CTPA. This explains the peripheral edema and the abdominal pain from congestive hepatopathy. NT-proBNP (432 pg/mL) and high-sensitivity troponin T (31 ng/L) were modestly elevated, consistent with myocardial strain rather than acute infarction; preserved LV systolic function and the absence of ventricular scar on MRI argue against a primary ischemic, infiltrative (amyloid/sarcoid) or inflammatory ventricular cardiomyopathy.

ALTERNATIVES EXCLUDED: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and CTEPH were excluded by the normal PVR and negative CTPA. Severe primary mitral regurgitation was excluded by echocardiography (only mild MR) — the giant V waves are explained by the large stroke volume entering a non-compliant, mechanically silent left atrium during profound bradycardia. Thyroid, electrolyte, digoxin, Lyme and amyloid studies were unavailable in this case, but the direct demonstration of an inexcitable, scarred atrium on EP study and cardiac MRI is diagnostic of atrial standstill regardless.

CLINICAL IMPLICATION: This is symptomatic bradycardia with heart failure — a Class I indication for permanent pacing. Because the atria are electrically silent and unpacable, an atrial lead would be futile; a single-chamber ventricular (VVI/R) pacemaker is required, with consideration of rate-responsive programming and diuretic therapy for congestion.

dx_agent: Spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture of a continent urinary reservoir (ileal neobladder/pouch) secondary to catheter drainage failure, presenting as acute peritonitis with cardiopulmonary decompensation and complicated by post-operative sepsis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa pouch colonisation)
reasoning:
The patient presented with severe lower abdominal pain and dyspnoea immediately following failure of catheter drainage of a continent urinary pouch — the classic mechanism for reservoir over-distension and rupture, since an obstructed or non-draining catheter allows intraluminal pressure to rise until the pouch wall gives way.

Contrast-enhanced CT performed with retrograde pouch contrast provided the definitive diagnosis: a large left laterodorsal reservoir defect with extravasation of contrast into the peritoneal cavity and free intraperitoneal fluid. This is diagnostic of intraperitoneal pouch rupture rather than a contained/extra-peritoneal leak. Emergency exploratory laparotomy independently confirmed pouch rupture, which was surgically repaired, with re-siting/fixation of the pouch catheter and nasogastric decompression.

The laboratory trajectory fits the pathophysiology precisely. Pre-operatively the WCC was elevated (15.3 x10^9/L) with reactive thrombocytosis (platelets 513 x10^9/L), while creatinine (1.08 mg/dL, eGFR 68) and CRP (1.7 mg/L) were normal. The normal creatinine argues against obstructive uropathy with acute kidney injury, and against prolonged urinary ascites with peritoneal creatinine reabsorption, indicating a hyper-acute mechanical event; the normal CRP indicates that frank infection had not yet been established at presentation. The dyspnoea and recorded cardiopulmonary decompensation are explained by urine-induced chemical peritonitis with abdominal distension and diaphragmatic splinting, together with the early systemic inflammatory response.

Post-operatively the patient developed sepsis: ICU day 1 lactate 4.7 mmol/L, and ICU day 2 CRP 361 mg/L with procalcitonin 4.7 ng/mL. Two sets of blood cultures remained negative at five days, indicating the sepsis was driven by the intra-abdominal/urinary source rather than bacteraemia. Pouch urine on day 7 grew low-concentration Pseudomonas aeruginosa, consistent with colonisation of the diverted urinary reservoir and the likely organism seeding the peritoneal cavity at the time of rupture.

Alternative diagnoses were considered and excluded: simple catheter obstruction with acute kidney injury and pulmonary oedema (excluded by normal creatinine and by CT demonstrating a structural pouch defect); peritoneal dialysis catheter malfunction or peritonitis (excluded — the catheter in question drains a urinary reservoir, and CT/laparotomy identified a pouch wall defect); primary hollow-viscus perforation such as diverticular or appendiceal perforation (excluded by retrograde pouch contrast demonstrating the leak originating from the reservoir, and by operative findings); and abdominal compartment syndrome as a primary event (a secondary contributor at most, with the rupture being the index lesion).

In summary, this is a spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture of a continent ileal urinary reservoir precipitated by catheter drainage failure, managed by emergency laparotomy and repair, and complicated by post-operative sepsis from a Pseudomonas-colonised pouch.

dx_agent: Extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma presenting with a recurrent right-sided chylothorax due to malignant mediastinal/thoracic duct lymphatic obstruction
reasoning:
Presentation: recurrent dyspnea within days of therapeutic drainage of a right pleural effusion, with tachypnea (no hypoxemia) and reduced right-sided breath sounds; repeat imaging confirmed recurrent right pleural effusion, and repeat thoracentesis drained 1.2 L.

Step 1 — Characterize the effusion. The fluid was grossly milky. Pleural fluid triglycerides were 434 mg/dL (well above the ~110 mg/dL diagnostic threshold), with cholesterol 154 mg/dL and a lymphocyte-predominant (82%) picture, pH 7.48, protein 2.4 g/dL and LDH 83 U/L. This is diagnostic of a CHYLOTHORAX. Gram stain and culture were negative, and pH was not acidic, excluding empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion. Cytology was negative for malignant cells, indicating the effusion is not a direct malignant (pleural-seeding) effusion but rather secondary to upstream lymphatic obstruction. The low protein/LDH (transudative-range) chemistry further argues against direct pleural tumour involvement or exudative inflammatory/infective causes.

Step 2 — Identify the cause of the chyle leak. Non-traumatic chylothorax is most often due to thoracic duct obstruction/infiltration by malignancy (lymphoma, carcinoma), or to sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or high central venous pressure states (cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, SVC obstruction). Contrast-enhanced CT chest showed bilateral hilar and mediastinal adenopathy with severe right-middle-lobe bronchial narrowing, partial atelectasis and infiltrates — i.e., bulky mediastinal nodal disease capable of both compressing the airway and obstructing thoracic duct drainage.

Step 3 — Obtain tissue. Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of the mediastinal/hilar nodes established EXTENSIVE-STAGE SMALL CELL LUNG CARCINOMA. This provides the definitive unifying diagnosis: SCLC with bulky mediastinal nodal involvement obstructing thoracic duct/lymphatic drainage, producing a rapidly re-accumulating right chylothorax and hence recurrent dyspnea days after each drainage.

Negative/limited data: pleural fluid cytology negative (expected — chyle leak is mechanical, not from pleural metastatic seeding); pleural fluid culture negative; abdominal CT, urinalysis, echocardiography, ECG, and serum chemistry panels were not available in this case, but the tissue diagnosis supersedes the need to pursue cirrhotic, cardiac, nephrotic or lymphomatous alternatives.

Clinical implications: management requires systemic chemotherapy (platinum–etoposide, with consideration of immunotherapy) as the definitive means of relieving the lymphatic obstruction, plus supportive measures for the chyle leak (repeat drainage/indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis, low-fat/MCT diet, octreotide), airway assessment for the right-middle-lobe bronchial narrowing, and completion of staging including brain MRI. Prognosis is driven by the extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma.

dx_agent: Metastatic malignant melanoma of unknown primary presenting as a malignant pleural effusion with diffuse pleural metastases (melanoma of the pleura)
reasoning:
Presentation: One week of dyspnea and new dry cough. Examination showed hypoxemia requiring 4 L/min nasal oxygen, diminished left basal breath sounds, and diffuse fine inspiratory crackles, with no palpable lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, and — importantly — no suspicious cutaneous or ocular primary lesion.

Laboratory: Mild thrombocytosis with normal inflammatory markers and unremarkable liver, thyroid, and renal function, arguing against bacterial pneumonia or a primarily infectious/inflammatory cause.

Imaging: Post-contrast chest CT demonstrated a moderate left pleural effusion with nodular circumferential pleural thickening including the mediastinal pleura — a pattern characteristic of malignant pleural disease. FDG PET-CT showed intensely avid circumferential pleural disease and identified no cutaneous or subcutaneous primary site.

Definitive tissue diagnosis: High-volume thoracentesis with pleural fluid cytology and immunohistochemistry revealed atypical epithelioid and spindle cells that were positive for SOX10, Melan-A, and S100, confirming melanocytic lineage. The cells were negative for calretinin and WT1 (excluding malignant pleural mesothelioma, the principal radiologic mimic given the circumferential nodular pleural thickening), negative for EMA (further arguing against mesothelioma/adenocarcinoma), and negative for p40 (excluding squamous carcinoma).

Synthesis: The immunophenotype is diagnostic of malignant melanoma. Because thorough dermatologic and ocular examination plus whole-body PET-CT identified no primary lesion, this represents metastatic melanoma of unknown primary — a well-recognized entity attributable to spontaneous regression of a primary cutaneous lesion or to a primary arising in an occult site (nodal, mucosal, or visceral). Isolated or dominant pleural involvement is an uncommon but described presentation of metastatic melanoma and closely mimics mesothelioma radiologically, making immunohistochemistry essential.

Clinical correlation: The dyspnea and dry cough are explained by the malignant pleural effusion and restrictive pleural encasement, with the diffuse crackles and hypoxemia reflecting associated parenchymal/lymphangitic involvement. The absence of fever and normal inflammatory markers are consistent with a neoplastic rather than infectious process.

Further management considerations (not required for diagnosis): molecular testing for BRAF V600E/K, NRAS, and KIT mutations to guide targeted therapy; contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude CNS metastases; and initiation of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (e.g., anti-PD-1 based regimen) with consideration of an indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis for symptomatic effusion control.

dx_agent: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) secondary to bilateral adrenal tuberculosis (tuberculous adrenalitis), presenting as calcified bilateral adrenal nodules
reasoning:
The patient presented with bilateral adrenal nodules and biochemical concern for adrenal insufficiency. Physical examination revealed hyperpigmentation over the hand interphalangeal joints and knees, indicating ACTH excess and therefore a primary (adrenal) rather than central cause.

Biochemistry confirmed primary adrenal insufficiency: markedly elevated plasma ACTH (577.10 ng/L, later 365.80 ng/L) paired with inappropriately low serum cortisol (161.00 nmol/L, later 139.00 nmol/L), accompanied by hyponatraemia and low fasting glucose — the classic electrolyte and metabolic consequences of combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency.

Contrast-enhanced adrenal CT demonstrated bilateral adrenal nodules WITH CALCIFICATION, together with old tuberculosis lesions in the lungs and pleura. Adrenal calcification in the setting of prior pulmonary/pleural TB is the hallmark radiological pattern of tuberculous adrenalitis, and immediately raised TB above the competing differentials (metastatic disease, primary adrenal lymphoma, bilateral adrenal haemorrhage, fungal infection such as histoplasmosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, and ACTH-driven macronodular hyperplasia or congenital adrenal hyperplasia).

The aetiology was then confirmed on three independent axes: (1) T-SPOT.TB positive, demonstrating M. tuberculosis sensitisation; (2) ultrasound-guided left adrenal biopsy showing necrotizing (caseating) granulomatous inflammation, the characteristic histopathology of TB; and (3) M. tuberculosis qPCR detecting mycobacterial DNA directly in the adrenal biopsy tissue, which is definitive. The negative acid-fast and silver stains do not undermine the diagnosis, as caseous paucibacillary material is frequently smear-negative; tissue PCR is more sensitive. Granulomatous histology with negative fungal staining also argues against histoplasmosis, and the histology excludes metastatic carcinoma and lymphoma.

Taken together — hyperpigmentation, high ACTH with low cortisol, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia, bilaterally calcified adrenal masses, prior pulmonary/pleural TB, positive IGRA, necrotizing granulomas on adrenal biopsy, and positive adrenal tissue MTB PCR — the diagnosis is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) caused by bilateral adrenal tuberculosis.

Management requires lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone in divided doses) with mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone), patient education on sick-day rules, an emergency steroid card/bracelet, and stress-dose parenteral hydrocortisone during intercurrent illness or surgery; plus a full course of standard anti-tuberculous chemotherapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol with pyridoxine) under infectious-disease supervision, with monitoring for drug interactions and contact screening. Note that adrenal calcification and adrenal failure are typically irreversible even after successful anti-TB treatment, so steroid replacement remains lifelong.

dx_agent: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Coombs/DAT-positive, IgG 2+ and C3d 5+) with spherocytic haemolysis and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemic jaundice
reasoning:
Presentation: progressive jaundice, dark (pigment-rich) stools, lethargy and lightheadedness; examination showed a pale, deeply icteric, afebrile patient with tachycardia (HR 92) and preserved blood pressure — the pallor-plus-jaundice combination is the hallmark of haemolytic anaemia rather than hepatobiliary disease.

Evidence for haemolysis: LDH markedly elevated at 1214 U/L; haptoglobin undetectable (<0.3 g/L), indicating consumption by free intravascular haemoglobin; total bilirubin 61 µmol/L with 72% unconjugated (indirect) fraction, consistent with haem catabolism and excluding obstructive/hepatocellular conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; marked reticulocytosis (261.7 ×10⁹/L, 23.7%) demonstrating an appropriate regenerative marrow response; peripheral film showing spherocytes with reticulocytosis and reactive neutrophilia, typical of splenic macrophage-mediated partial phagocytosis of antibody-coated red cells. Lactate 4.2 mmol/L reflects impaired tissue oxygen delivery from the anaemia.

Evidence for an immune mechanism: the direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG (2+) and complement C3d (5+). A positive DAT distinguishes this from non-immune causes of spherocytosis (hereditary spherocytosis, which is DAT-negative), from microangiopathic haemolysis (no schistocytes reported), and from G6PD deficiency or other enzyme/membrane defects. The IgG-predominant coating with spherocytes and extravascular haemolysis localises the process to warm-reactive autoantibodies acting at body temperature with splenic sequestration, i.e. warm AIHA (the mixed IgG + C3d pattern occurs in a substantial minority of warm AIHA cases); cold agglutinin disease typically gives isolated C3d positivity with red-cell agglutination rather than spherocytes.

Differential diagnoses excluded: obstructive jaundice/choledocholithiasis and hepatitis (bilirubin predominantly unconjugated, no fever or biliary pain, transaminases/ALP not flagged); gastrointestinal bleeding with melena (stools dark from excess stercobilin/urobilinogen rather than tarry melaena, and bleeding would not produce a positive DAT, spherocytes or unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia); hereditary spherocytosis (DAT positive); TTP/HUS/DIC (no schistocytes, no renal or neurological findings, no coagulopathy reported).

Limitations: microbiology (Mycoplasma, EBV, hepatitis, HIV), urine studies, abdominal ultrasound, ANA, cold agglutinin titre and serum protein electrophoresis were not available in this case record, so a secondary trigger (lymphoproliferative disorder, SLE, drug exposure or infection) could not be formally identified; the case is therefore classified as DAT-positive warm AIHA, with secondary causes to be excluded prospectively.

Management implications: immediate corticosteroids (prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg/day), folic acid supplementation, transfusion of least-incompatible crossmatched blood if haemodynamically compromised, VTE prophylaxis given the prothrombotic state of active haemolysis, and second-line rituximab or splenectomy for steroid-refractory disease, alongside a search for an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder.

dx_agent: Spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma (cervicothoracic, C6–T2) causing acute spinal cord compression with complete paraplegia (ASIA A) and bowel/bladder incontinence — neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent decompressive laminectomy and hematoma evacuation.
reasoning:
Presentation: acute interscapular pain followed by rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness and bowel/bladder incontinence — the classic temporal sequence of an acute compressive myelopathy, with pain at the level of the lesion preceding cord dysfunction.

Physical examination localised the lesion precisely: leg strength 0/5 with arm strength 5/5 places the lesion in the thoracic/low-cervical cord (below the C5–T1 myotomes supplying the arms); absent perianal sensation indicates loss of sacral sensation with NO sacral sparing, i.e. a functionally complete cord syndrome (ASIA A); the preserved bulbocavernosus reflex demonstrates an intact S2–S4 reflex arc, confirming an upper motor neuron/cord lesion above the conus rather than a cauda equina or conus medullaris lesion. This combination excludes peripheral/root causes and mandates urgent cord imaging.

Differential considered: spinal epidural hematoma, spinal epidural abscess, metastatic epidural cord compression, anterior spinal artery infarction/aortic dissection, and acute transverse myelitis.

MRI of the cervicothoracic spine was the decisive investigation and demonstrated an epidural hematoma compressing the cord and posterior thecal sac from C6 to T2, with no traumatic or structural lesion — confirming the diagnosis and excluding abscess, tumour, and intrinsic myelopathy.

Supporting laboratory data: normal platelets (250,000/µL), PT 12 s/INR 1.0, and aPTT 30 s exclude a coagulopathy or anticoagulant-related cause, establishing the hemorrhage as SPONTANEOUS. The mild leukocytosis (13,000/µL with 85% neutrophils) is consistent with an acute stress response rather than infection, and in the absence of fever or an epidural collection on MRI does not support epidural abscess.

Clinical significance: spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma with a complete deficit is time-critical. Neurological recovery is strongly dependent on the interval to decompression, so the patient requires immediate neurosurgical decompressive laminectomy and evacuation of the hematoma, with adjunctive measures (urinary catheterisation, consideration of corticosteroids, VTE prophylaxis timing balanced against the hemorrhage, and nil by mouth for theatre). Prognosis for motor recovery is guarded given the complete (0/5, no sacral sparing) deficit, but urgent surgery offers the only chance of meaningful recovery and prevents further ascending compromise at the cervicothoracic junction.

dx_agent: Foreign-body-induced mechanical small-bowel obstruction with peritonitis — ingested sharp/linear foreign body causing small-bowel obstruction and suspected perforation/strangulation (surgical emergency requiring urgent laparotomy)
reasoning:
The patient presented with the classic triad of progressively worsening diffuse abdominal pain, distension and nausea, indicating an obstructive abdominal process. Physical examination demonstrated signs of peritoneal irritation, establishing peritonitis and raising immediate concern for perforation or bowel ischaemia rather than simple, uncomplicated obstruction.

The provisional differential at that stage included perforated hollow viscus (peptic ulcer, diverticular, appendiceal), mechanical small-bowel obstruction progressing to strangulation or perforation (adhesions, hernia, neoplasm, foreign body), acute mesenteric ischaemia, severe acute pancreatitis, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Targeted investigation was therefore directed at identifying free intraluminal/extraluminal air, defining the level and cause of obstruction, and assessing for ischaemia.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast was diagnostic: multiple small-bowel air–fluid levels together with a linear hyperdense intraluminal structure consistent with a foreign body, with mechanical obstruction suspected. An upright abdominal radiograph independently corroborated the obstruction, showing multiple small-bowel air–fluid levels. The direct identification of a linear hyperdense intraluminal foreign body at the site of obstruction unifies the entire presentation and effectively excludes alternative mechanical causes (adhesions, hernia, tumour) as well as medical mimics such as pancreatitis or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Crucially, the presence of peritonitis on examination in the setting of a sharp, linear impacted foreign body indicates transmural bowel injury — that is, foreign-body perforation and/or strangulation of the obstructed loop — rather than a simple obstructive ileus. Although no free subdiaphragmatic air was reported on the plain film, plain radiography has limited sensitivity for perforation and cannot exclude it; the CT and clinical findings take precedence.

Laboratory studies (CBC, CRP, lactate, metabolic panel, liver function tests, lipase/amylase, coagulation, blood gas, procalcitonin), bedside studies (vital signs, ECG), erect chest radiography, blood cultures and urinalysis were all unavailable in this published case, so no biochemical confirmation of sepsis, ischaemia or organ dysfunction could be obtained. The diagnosis therefore rests on the concordant examination and imaging findings, which are themselves sufficient and specific.

Management is urgent: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric flora, analgesia, immediate surgical consultation for laparotomy with foreign-body extraction and resection or repair of the compromised bowel segment, and close serial reassessment for sepsis and further perforation.

dx_agent: Ruptured/bleeding primary abdominal ectopic pregnancy implanted on the omentum in the left upper quadrant (perisplenic, between spleen and descending colon), with hemoperitoneum — presenting as worsening left upper abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
reasoning:
A woman of reproductive age presented with worsening left upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Examination showed isolated left upper abdominal tenderness with stable vitals (BP 107/77, HR 89, afebrile), no lower abdominal tenderness or peritonism, no vaginal bleeding, a closed cervix, and no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness.

Serum hCG was 10,130 IU/L, confirming pregnancy and lying far above the discriminatory zone (~1,500–3,500 IU/L) at which an intrauterine gestational sac should be demonstrable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed NO intrauterine gestational sac, an endometrial thickness of only 8 mm, and no adnexal abnormality — establishing a pregnancy of unknown location with a very high likelihood of ectopic gestation.

The atypical location of the pain (left upper quadrant rather than pelvic) prompted upper abdominal imaging. Noncontrast CT demonstrated a 21 × 19 × 10 mm indeterminate left upper abdominal lesion, and contrast CT characterised this as a vascular left upper abdominal mass measuring 46 × 40 × 56 mm — consistent with a vascularised trophoblastic implantation rather than a simple cyst or hematoma.

Diagnostic laparoscopy provided the definitive answer: approximately 300 mL of hemoperitoneum with an actively bleeding 6 × 4 × 5 cm lesion situated between the spleen and the descending colon and involving the omentum, while the uterus, both ovaries and both fallopian tubes appeared entirely normal.

This fulfils Studdiford's criteria for a PRIMARY ABDOMINAL PREGNANCY: (1) normal fallopian tubes and ovaries with no evidence of tubal or ovarian pregnancy, (2) absence of a uteroplacental fistula, and (3) a gestation attached exclusively to a peritoneal/omental surface. The normal tubes and ovaries exclude tubal and ovarian ectopic pregnancy; the empty uterus with hCG >10,000 excludes a viable intrauterine pregnancy and makes completed miscarriage implausible given the rising symptomatic picture and the visualised vascular mass. Splenic pathology (infarct, rupture, splenic artery aneurysm) and pancreatitis were considered but are excluded by the laparoscopic identification of a bleeding omental gestational mass with normal pelvic organs and by the CT demonstration of a discrete vascular lesion separate from the splenic parenchyma.

The hemoperitoneum with active bleeding explains the worsening pain and the gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea/vomiting from peritoneal blood irritation). This is an immediate surgical emergency requiring operative excision of the abdominal pregnancy with haemostasis, careful management of the placental/omental attachment site given the risk of torrential haemorrhage, resuscitation and blood product availability, and anti-D immunoglobulin if the patient is Rh-negative.
